{{One source|date=December 2022}}
The '''Jacobi bound problem''' concerns the veracity of Jacobi's inequality which is an [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]] on the [[absolute dimension]] of a [[differential algebraic variety]] in terms of its defining equations.
This is one of [[Kolchin's Problems]].

The inequality is the differential algebraic analog of [[Bézout's theorem]] in affine space. 
Although first formulated by [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi|Jacobi]], In 1936 [[Joseph Ritt]] recognized the problem as non-rigorous in that Jacobi didn't even have a rigorous notion of absolute dimension (Jacobi and Ritt used the term "order" - which Ritt first gave a rigorous definition for using the notion of [[transcendence degree]]). 
Intuitively, the absolute dimension is the number of constants of integration required to specify a solution of a system of [[ordinary differential equation]]s.
A [[mathematical proof]] of the inequality has been open since 1936. 

==Statement==
Let <math> (K,\partial) </math> be a [[differential field]] of characteristic zero and consider <math> \Gamma </math> a differential algebraic variety determined by the vanishing of differential polynomials <math> u_1,\ldots,u_n \in K\lbrace x_1,\ldots,x_n\rbrace </math>. 
If <math> \Gamma_1 </math> is an irreducible component of <math> \Gamma </math> of finite absolute dimension then 

<math> a(\Gamma_1) \leq J(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_n). </math>

In the above display <math> J(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_n) </math> is the *jacobi number*. 
It is defined to be 

<math> \max_{\sigma \in S_n} \sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{ord}_{x_i}^{\partial}(u_{\sigma(i)}) </math>.
